statement: In college students, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), evidence is insufficient to say whether using more protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver), compared with using fewer, lowers drinking or alcohol-related problems. Students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. Asked how often they used strategies when they drank, students who reported more said they drank less (negative correlations in three studies in one paper by the author's team), and in three studies students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems; the review gives the size of almost none of these links. Over time the links were weaker or mixed: in one study 3 of 9 correlations with later problems were not significant; in another, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; in women, strategies reported at the start went with fewer problems 4 months later but not with drinking at the same time. In two studies of day-by-day reports (one a 15-day diary of 40 students), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, part of the fall in drinking or problems was statistically explained by a rise in reported strategy use (mediation); in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In surveys of college students, those who said they used safety habits more often when drinking tended to say they drank less, but most studies asked about habits and drinking at the same time. Day by day, students drank more on days they had a designated driver or went home with a friend, which the review's author thinks happens because these are planned for nights of heavy drinking. Telling students to use more habits did not make them drink less in the one study that tried it, so whether the habits themselves lower drinking or harm is not known.
population: College students in 62 published quantitative studies found up to February 2013 (some samples appear in more than one study; countries not reported in the review), including incoming students, athletes, women and students sent to alcohol programmes, as summarized by one narrative review
exposure: Self-reported use of alcohol protective behavioural strategies, measured with at least 11 questionnaires in many versions (most often the Protective Behavioral Strategies Survey): strategies used just before, during or after drinking, such as setting a limit or leaving at a set time, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, drinking water, eating, avoiding drinking games or mixing types of alcohol, keeping track of drinks, using a designated driver or going home with a friend; 13 of the 62 studies also counted avoiding drinking altogether
comparator: Students reporting fewer strategies (between people, mostly cross-sectional); days without a given strategy (within people, two studies); control groups in trials of brief interventions, where strategy use was a measured mediator, not what was randomized; no instruction to use strategies (one experiment)
outcome: Self-reported alcohol use (amount, frequency, heavy drinking, estimated blood alcohol) and alcohol-related problems
magnitude: No pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: negative correlations with drinking in 3 studies using a how-often-when-drinking scale, and positive ones with a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions; a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant (1 study); day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).

risk_of_bias.note: Strategies and outcomes self-reported, nearly always retrospectively at the same sitting and often with no time window; mostly between-person cross-sectional data; the review summarizes what the author judged the most distinctive significant findings of each study, without appraising them; the author co-wrote 7 of the 62 studies (editors' count), including the day-by-day evidence (card sc_pearson_2013).

inconsistency.note: Direction differs by strategy and design: less drinking between people, but more drinking and more problems day by day with serious harm reduction and limiting or stopping strategies; mediation in three trials and no change in strategy use in three; one null instruction experiment.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: every anchor is a narrative review's account of primary studies not read here; college students only; strategies measured in bundles, not one at a time.

imprecision.note: Not assessable: the review gives almost no effect or sample sizes.

publication_bias.note: Published studies only; not assessed by the review.

grade.reasoning: Mostly cross-sectional observational evidence starts low (in the trials the interventions were randomized, but strategy use was a measured mediator); rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness, giving very low, the floor. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3). Insufficient evidence rather than 'is associated with': the review gives no sizes for the links, and their direction depends on the strategy and on whether students are compared with each other or with themselves on other days. Status mixed: findings point different ways, with only the author's untested explanation. The 2026 meta-analysis of randomized trials of protective strategies among adults (Van Nhat et al.) is on the reading list and has not been read; it would replace this review for the trial evidence.

statement: In people who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel 'designer' benzodiazepines, most often together with opioids, stimulants or alcohol), evidence is insufficient to say whether any harm reduction service or policy lowers harm. As described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources found up to July 2025, which mapped them without appraising them (Morrison et al., 2025), the approaches studied were drug checking (11 sources), prescribed benzodiazepines as treatment or safer supply (5), policies on scheduling, prescribing and surveillance (9) and approaches for particular groups (10); by the designs listed in the review's table, 17 were quantitative pilot, retrospective, cross-sectional or similar studies, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews and 1 a policy analysis, and none was a randomized trial. Most drug-checking sources tested how well laboratory methods detect benzodiazepines: in 59 samples, a portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometer identified 36% of those containing etizolam (78% when etizolam was more than 3% of the sample by weight), against 9% with infrared spectroscopy. At one Canadian service, infrared analysis found alprazolam in 33 of 139 samples (23.7%) that people expected to be alprazolam (Xanax), and of 20 sent for confirmatory testing, 14 contained other active ingredients only. In a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, among 68 of 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore followed up a month after receiving fentanyl test strips, reported using alone fell from 96% to 68% and benzodiazepine use from 22% to 7%. Prescribed benzodiazepines were described for 6 of 77 residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, whose programme as a whole reported no overdoses, and for more than 70 people experiencing homelessness in Dublin, from whom no feedback was collected; in one inner-London general practice, opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines (127 of 278) stayed in treatment longer (72 months against 34 and 51) and had a lower death rate in treatment (1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years) than the others, but a larger rise in deaths after leaving treatment, by figures the review reports inconsistently. After Australia moved alprazolam to a stricter schedule in 2014, four of five evaluations summarized in a 2021 review reported large falls in alprazolam use and harms, including overdose deaths, while figures the authors cite from a letter, without definitions, show benzodiazepine overdose deaths overall rising from 160 in 2009 to 238 in 2015. After the United Kingdom rescheduled temazepam gel capsules, 100 people interviewed described less injecting of capsules but continued injecting of tablets, higher prices and substitution with flunitrazepam. The authors find harm reduction largely missing for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Drug checking, prescribed benzos and stricter rules have all been tried for people who use benzos, but none has been tested in a way that shows whether it lowers harm. Checking found that many samples people thought were Xanax held other drugs, and some testing methods often missed 'designer' benzos.
population: People who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel), most also using opioids, stimulants or alcohol, in 35 sources gathered by one scoping review: drug samples at checking services, clients of harm reduction services, women who do sex work, residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, people in treatment, emergency-department and festival patients, forum posters and poison-centre callers
exposure: Harm reduction services and policies: drug checking, prescribed benzodiazepines (agonist treatment or safer supply), rescheduling, prescribing rules, toxicosurveillance and a poison-centre line
comparator: Mostly none; a few observational comparisons (patients maintained on benzodiazepines against others; positive against negative test results), before-and-after measurements without a control group, and one laboratory method against another
outcome: Detection of benzodiazepines in drug samples; reported behaviour after testing; treatment retention and mortality; prescribing, use and deaths after policy changes; people's accounts
magnitude: No pooled estimates. Detection: portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometry 36% of etizolam-containing samples (78% above 3% by weight) against 9% with infrared (59 samples); a miniature mass spectrometer quantified etizolam in 11 of 15 samples that strips and/or infrared had failed to detect or quantify. Expected alprazolam: 33 of 139 (23.7%) by infrared; of 20 confirmed, 2 alprazolam alone, 4 alprazolam with other ingredients, 14 other ingredients only. Toronto: benzodiazepine-type drugs in 116 of 555 samples, 15 of them expected to be benzodiazepines; benzodiazepine-type drugs present in 24 (41%) of samples linked to a negative effect (presence, not cause). After test strips (pilot, 68 of 103 followed up): using alone 96% to 68%, benzodiazepine use 22% to 7%; 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour. Prescribed benzodiazepines: 6 of 77 hotel residents; more than 70 people in Dublin. Opioid substitution case notes: retention 72 against 34 and 51 months; in-treatment mortality 1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years; post-treatment rate in the maintained group 5.90 per 100 years, reported as a 450% rise (4.5 times the in-treatment rate, an increase of about 350%, editors' calculation). Alprazolam rescheduling: 4 of 5 evaluations reported large declines; alprazolam-related deaths 57 (2012) to 23 (2015); benzodiazepine overdose deaths 160 (2009) to 238 (2015). Kentucky 'no benzodiazepine' formulary: prescriptions down 89% over two years. Victoria emergency departments, 2020 to 2022: novel benzodiazepine-type drugs in 183 of 1112 drug-toxicity presentations (16.5%). Poison-centre line: safety information to 6635 of 17,616 callers (37.7%), no outcome evaluation.

statement: In people who use benzodiazepines, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything they do themselves before or during use lowers harm: as described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources that did not appraise them (Morrison et al., 2025), no source compared people who used such a practice with people who did not. Practices appear only as people's accounts or researchers' recommendations: in a study of a Swedish online drug forum about flubromazolam (122 in the review's table), posters described limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they used, avoiding alcohol at the same time and comparing vendors and batches; in British Columbia during COVID-19, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs (45, interviewed) formed informal peer networks to check on one another because of benzodiazepine contamination and the risk of sexual assault; in an ethnography in Melbourne, one participant described using temazepam at home to avoid losing money or drugs, or being arrested, while sedated; and the authors of a survey of 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok called for education against injecting alone. The only numbers come from a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, in which 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore received fentanyl test strips: of the 68 followed up a month later, 69% reported doing something to lower harm after a result, such as asking someone to check on them, and reported using alone fell from 96% to 68%. The review searched on terms such as harm reduction and did not cover peer-led resources, so practices described elsewhere may be missing; its authors find harm reduction largely absent for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: People who use benzos describe staying at home, keeping the drug out of reach while high, avoiding alcohol at the same time and having friends check on them. No study found by a 2025 review compared people who do these things with people who do not, so it is not known whether any of them lowers harm.
population: People who use benzodiazepines, including novel ones, in forum, interview, ethnographic, survey and pilot sources gathered by one scoping review: posters on a Swedish drug forum; 45 women and gender-diverse people who use drugs in British Columbia; one participant in Melbourne; 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok; 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore

statement: In one randomized, double-blind crossover trial in a laboratory, 18 healthy adults who had used cannabis before but not in the previous 30 days (the completers of 22 randomized; Zamarripa et al., 2023) each ate, in random order on days at least a week apart, a placebo brownie, a brownie with a THC-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC, no CBD) and a brownie with a CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD), and swallowed a cocktail of five probe medicines, including the sedative midazolam, 30 minutes later in every session (study conditions only). Compared with the THC-dominant brownie, the CBD-dominant brownie was associated with higher blood levels of THC and of 11-OH-THC, a substance the body makes from THC (peaks 14.8 against 8.2 and 53.9 against 4.5, units not printed in the text: about 1.8 and 12 times higher, editors' arithmetic), and with stronger effects. Peak ratings on 0–100 scales, made by the participants without knowing which brownie they had eaten, were higher for drug effect (72.8 against 59.2), unpleasant (38.6 against 19.6), feeling sick (26.1 against 11.6), memory trouble (37.8 against 27.4) and difficulty with routine tasks (46.7 against 30.3); scores on an arithmetic task and a divided-attention task were worse (P = .049 and .04), and heart rate rose more (by 25.4 against 10.1 beats a minute). Pleasant and liking ratings did not differ significantly, and anxious (23.9 against 13.3), paranoid (23.4 against 12.0) and sleepy (42.6 against 21.0) ratings, though higher than after placebo, did not differ significantly from the THC-dominant brownie. The placebo brownie with the probe medicines changed no effect measure significantly. Effects were followed for 24 hours: the strongest drug effect came later on average (2.9 against 2.1 hours after the probe medicines; not tested statistically) and total THC exposure (area under the curve) was about 2.5 times higher (editors' arithmetic), but how long the stronger effects lasted is not given in the parts of the paper that could be read. In these conditions the CBD-dominant extract did not soften THC's effects, which the authors present as contrary to common claims that CBD dampens THC's unwanted effects; whether the difference came from CBD, from the extract's other cannabinoids or from changed levels of the probe medicines, which the paper does not report, cannot be told, and smaller amounts of CBD, CBD taken at another time, smoked or vaped cannabis and regular cannabis use were not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one lab trial, 18 healthy adults ate brownies with THC alone or with the same THC plus a large amount of CBD. With CBD, blood THC was higher, and people felt the drug more, felt sicker, had more trouble with memory and simple tasks, and had a faster heartbeat, without liking it more. Other test medicines were given at the same time, so it is not certain what caused the difference, and the trial did not test smaller amounts of CBD or smoked cannabis.
population: 18 healthy adults aged 18 to 50 (11 men, 7 women; mean age 30) with past cannabis use but none in the 30 days before the first session (mean 124 days since last use), completers among 22 randomized, at the Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, United States
exposure: A brownie with a CBD-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD; the extract also held about 2% CBC and 1% CBG), followed 30 minutes later by a cocktail of five probe medicines (caffeine, omeprazole, losartan, dextromethorphan, midazolam) (study conditions only)
comparator: The same participants after a brownie with a THC-dominant extract carrying the same nominal THC dose (20 mg THC, no detectable CBD) and after a placebo brownie, each with the same probe cocktail
outcome: Plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH; peak self-ratings on the Drug Effect Questionnaire (0–100), cognitive task performance and heart rate over 24 hours
magnitude: CBD-dominant against THC-dominant extract, mean (SD): THC peak 14.8 (5.5) against 8.2 (4.0), area under the curve 84.9 (29.38) against 33.3 (16.9); 11-OH-THC peak 53.9 (22.6) against 4.5 (1.9), area 349.0 (137.1) against 34.0 (16.4); all P < .001; units not printed in the text (editors' arithmetic: THC peak about 1.8 and area about 2.5 times, 11-OH-THC peak about 12 and area about 10 times higher). Peak change from baseline on 0–100 ratings, CBD-dominant against THC-dominant: drug effect 72.8 against 59.2; unpleasant 38.6 against 19.6; sick 26.1 against 11.6; dry or red eyes 28.8 against 15.9; memory 37.8 against 27.4; routine tasks 46.7 against 30.3 (all Tukey P < .05); anxious 23.9 against 13.3, paranoid 23.4 against 12.0, sleepy 42.6 against 21.0 (not significant). Paced serial addition -22.7 against -6.6 correct (P = .049); divided-attention error 32.7 against 15.9 (P = .04); heart rate +25.4 against +10.1 beats a minute (P = .001). Time of peak drug effect 2.9 against 2.1 hours (not tested). The printed Cohen's d values for the effects do not match the printed means and SDs and are not used.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 some concerns (card sc_zamarripa_2023): only completers analysed after 4 of 22 randomized participants dropped out and were replaced, with the reasons in a figure that could not be viewed; 36 outcomes without correction across outcomes; the abstract, text and table disagree on several effect results, and many printed effect sizes do not match the printed data.

indirectness.note: The probe cocktail, including the sedative midazolam and dextromethorphan, was taken in every session and its levels under each extract are not reported, so part of the extra impairment may come from it; the CBD-dominant extract also carried other cannabinoids; one large oral CBD amount, in healthy adults who did not use cannabis regularly.

imprecision.note: 18 people; the two task differences were at P = .049 and .04, and the printed intervals for the effects cannot be relied on.

publication_bias.note: Registered trial (NCT04201197); these are secondary outcomes.

grade.reasoning: Randomized, double-blind crossover comparisons start high (METHODS §6.3); rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low for the claim as worded, whose weakest necessary link is the stronger effects. The rise in blood THC and 11-OH-THC on its own is large, objective and precise and would rate low (high, minus risk of bias and indirectness). Worded as an association because the two extracts differed in more than CBD and the probe medicines may have contributed. Status single study: other trials of CBD with THC, mostly inhaled, a 2019 systematic review (Freeman et al.) and a 2026 meta-analysis of blood THC with CBD (Chester et al.) are on the reading list and have not been read; the answer may become contested when they are.
